title: Gemini 4 Argon Teaches Apollo Robot Cornhole via Zero-Shot Learning

tickers.name: Alphabet Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
A robotic system that can articulate its own internal reasoning and use gestures to explain its movements was recently showcased by Google DeepMind. The entity, an Apptronik Apollo humanoid, learned to play cornhole by observing a single human demonstration video via the Gemini 4 Argon model. This 'zero-shot' process included the autonomous generation of a simulation environment and system identification, which allowed the robot to sink 7 consecutive shots in a physical trial without prior task-specific training.

The pipeline reduces the time required for manual modeling of physical skills from several weeks to a few hours. By turning ordinary video into a training ground for AI, researchers suggest that the immense video library of YouTube could give Google a competitive advantage in developing physical AI without requiring the company to manufacture its own hardware. This shift in capabilities is currently altering fundamental assumptions regarding the development of robotic intelligence.

selectedTweets.text:
I’m still half in disbelief 
We asked Gemini Argon to teach the Apollo humanoid to play cornhole, and it zero-shotted it

All we gave it was a video of a person doing it. It then took control of the robot, generated its own sim env, performed some sysID, and trained launches on the real robot. 

It took it a few real shots to improve and then land many consecutive airmails. 

The process was so long and articulated that we asked the robot itself to explain what it did to us, as you can see at the end of the video. It even came up with the gestures

Great demo for a great model @googledeepmind @apptronik

selectedTweets.text:
In robotics, Gemini 4 Argon is speeding up real-world physical learning.

We let Argon watch a video of a human playing cornhole. It mapped the environment, calculated whole-body joint movements, and autonomously built the simulation code to practice.

When transferred to Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid, the robot sank seven straight shots in a real-world trial.
